clinicalPearls: These tumours do not cause a clinical hormone-excess syndrome, so they present late with mass-related symptoms or as incidental findings
Symptoms, when present, arise from local growth: abdominal pain, obstructive jaundice, a palpable mass or bleeding
They may still secrete peptides such as chromogranin A or pancreatic polypeptide that serve as tumour markers without producing a syndrome
An increasing proportion are discovered incidentally on cross-sectional imaging performed for other reasons
Somatostatin-receptor imaging with gallium DOTATATE is valuable for staging and detecting metastatic disease
Tumour grade, based on proliferative indices, and stage are the key determinants of behaviour and management
A significant subset are associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 and other inherited syndromes
Management ranges from surveillance of small low-grade lesions to surgical resection and systemic therapy including somatostatin analogues for advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Non-functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours arise from the neuroendocrine cells of the pancreatic islets but do not release hormones in amounts sufficient to produce a recognisable clinical syndrome. Because they are hormonally silent, they typically remain undetected until they grow large enough to cause local effects or metastasise, most often to regional lymph nodes and the liver. Their biological behaviour spans a spectrum from indolent, well-differentiated tumours to aggressive, poorly differentiated carcinomas, largely reflected in histological grade and stage. A meaningful minority occur in the context of hereditary syndromes, particularly multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, which favours multifocal disease.
additionalDifferentials: Functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour such as insulinoma or gastrinoma
Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm of the pancreas
Metastasis to the pancreas from another primary
Autoimmune or focal chronic pancreatitis forming a mass
additionalInvestigations: Cross-sectional imaging with contrast-enhanced computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging
Endoscopic ultrasound with tissue sampling for diagnosis and grading
Somatostatin-receptor imaging such as gallium DOTATATE positron emission tomography
Chromogranin A and, where relevant, pancreatic polypeptide as tumour markers
Screening for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 where indicated
redFlags: Obstructive jaundice or duodenal obstruction from local growth
Hepatic or extensive nodal metastases at diagnosis
Rapid tumour growth on surveillance imaging
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends chiefly on grade and stage; small, well-differentiated, resectable tumours have an excellent outlook, whereas high-grade or metastatic disease carries a considerably poorer prognosis, though indolent metastatic tumours may still be compatible with prolonged survival.
pitfalls: Assuming that absence of a hormone syndrome means the tumour is benign
Mistaking the lesion for pancreatic adenocarcinoma and misdirecting management
Failing to grade the tumour, which is central to prognosis and treatment
Overlooking associated multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
Neglecting somatostatin-receptor imaging and understaging metastatic disease
management: Resect localised tumours surgically by enucleation or formal pancreatectomy, while small low-grade incidental tumours may be followed with active surveillance
Use somatostatin analogues such as octreotide or lanreotide for antiproliferative control of advanced, well-differentiated, somatostatin-receptor-positive disease
Offer molecular targeted therapy — the mTOR inhibitor everolimus or the tyrosine kinase inhibitor sunitinib — for progressive advanced tumours
Consider peptide-receptor radionuclide therapy with lutetium-labelled DOTATATE for somatostatin-receptor-positive metastatic disease
Treat high-grade or poorly differentiated carcinoma with platinum-based chemotherapy, and use liver-directed approaches for hepatic metastases
Monitor with chromogranin A and serial cross-sectional and somatostatin-receptor imaging to track grade-based behaviour
Screen for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 and offer genetic counselling and family screening where hereditary disease is suspected
Manage within a specialist neuroendocrine tumour multidisciplinary team
